welcome.line: Come try a fictional story with me. You make the choices; we’ll see what happens.

caught.line: You and your accomplice Ravi robbed a jewellery store. You’ve been caught—and put in separate rooms.

goal.line: You want the fewest prison years for yourself. Ravi wants the fewest for himself.

actions.line: Accept the deal: confess and name Ravi. Or refuse it: stay silent. You control only your statement.

separate.line: No talking or agreements with Ravi. You each choose without seeing the other’s statement. Here’s the deal.

rule_ss.line: If you both stay silent, you each get one year.

rule_cs.line: You confess; Ravi stays silent. You get zero prison years—none. Ravi gets five.

rule_sc.line: You stay silent; Ravi confesses. You get five years. Ravi gets zero.

rule_cc.line: If you both confess, you each get three years. Ready to try it?

deal.line: Imagine Ravi stays silent. Silence gets you one year; confession gets you zero. What do you say?
deal.visual: Your prison yearsRavi stays silentSilent1 yearConfess0 years

silent.line: You stayed silent. So did Ravi: one year each. Now change only your statement.

flip_confess.line: Ravi stayed silent. Your confession cut your prison time from one year to zero.
flip_confess.visual: Two separate roomsBeforeYou 1 · Ravi 1After · you confessYouConfess1prison yearsRaviSilent1prison years

both.line: Imagine both confessing: three years each. Ravi keeps confessing. If only you stay silent, what happens to your years?

solo.line: You expected “Fall”. Your silence takes you from three years to five. Ravi keeps confessing: zero for him.
solo.visual: Two separate roomsBeforeYou 3 · Ravi 3After · only you stay silentYouSilent3prison yearsRaviConfess3prison years

ravi_only.line: Imagine three years each again. Only Ravi goes silent: five years for him, zero for you.
ravi_only.visual: Two separate roomsReset · beforeYou 3 · Ravi 3After · only Ravi stays silentYouConfess3prison yearsRaviSilent3prison years

joint_second.line: Imagine three years each again. Now both go silent: one year each. That took both statements changing.
joint_second.visual: Two separate roomsReset · beforeYou 3 · Ravi 3After · both stay silentYouSilent3prison yearRaviSilent3prison year

mirror.line: Look from Ravi’s side. You stay silent: his confession gets zero years; his silence gets one.
mirror.visual: Ravi’s prison yearsYou stay silentConfess0 yearsSilent1 year

mirror_confess.line: You confess: Ravi gets three years by confessing, five by staying silent. Confession cuts his time either way.
mirror_confess.visual: Ravi’s prison yearsYou confessConfess3 yearsSilent5 years

your_pressure.line: Same for you: confessing gives zero instead of one when Ravi’s silent; three instead of five when he confesses.
your_pressure.visual: Your prison yearsRavi silentConfess0 yearsSilent1 yearYour prison yearsRavi confessesConfess3 yearsSilent5 years

name.line: That’s the prisoner’s dilemma: confessing cuts your years, whichever statement Ravi makes. He faces the same pressure.

name_shared.line: Yet both confessing means three years each; both staying silent means one. Individually better choices can leave both worse off.
name_shared.visual: Two separate roomsBeforeBoth confess · 3 years eachAfter · both silentYouSilent3prison yearRaviSilent3prison year

name_best.line: One each beats three each—but zero beats one. And choosing your silence doesn’t choose Ravi’s.
name_best.visual: Your prison yearsRavi stays silentSilent1 yearConfess0 years

cafe_intro.line: Now imagine running a café beside another owner’s. Your goal: the most profit today—money left after costs.

cafe_rules.line: Choose discounts or usual prices without seeing the other’s choice. Only today counts; all costs are included.
cafe_rules.visual: Today’s profitYour caféUsual / discountOther caféUsual / discount

cafe_uu.line: When both cafés keep usual prices, you each make ₹5,000.
cafe_uu.visual: Today’s profitYour caféUsual prices₹5,000profitOther caféUsual prices₹5,000profit

cafe_du.line: You discount; they keep usual prices. You make ₹6,000. They make ₹2,000.

cafe_ud.line: You keep usual prices; they discount. You make ₹2,000. They make ₹6,000.

cafe_dd.line: When both cafés discount, you each make ₹3,000.

cafe.line: Imagine both discounting: ₹3,000 each. They keep discounting. What will your café do?

c_usual.line: You kept usual prices. They still discount. Your ₹3,000 drops to ₹2,000—only your café changed.

labels: Imagine their café at usual prices

c_shared.line: They discount: you earn ₹3,000 by discounting, ₹2,000 at usual prices. Discounting pays you more.

c_compare_usual.line: They keep usual prices: you earn ₹6,000 by discounting, ₹5,000 at usual prices. Discounting still pays more.
c_compare_usual.visual: Your profitOther café: usual pricesDiscount₹6,000Usual prices₹5,000

c_compare_both.line: They face the same choice. Yet both discounting earns ₹3,000 each; both keeping usual prices earns ₹5,000 each.

cost_intro.line: One change: every discount now costs an extra ₹2,000. Usual prices cost nothing extra. Everything else stays unchanged.

cost_uu.line: Both keeping usual prices means nothing extra to pay. You still make ₹5,000 each.

cost_ud.line: You keep usual prices; they discount. You earn ₹2,000. After the extra cost, they earn ₹4,000.

cost_dd.line: Both discounting means ₹3,000 minus ₹2,000: ₹1,000 each. That’s after the extra cost.

finish_both.line: Same for the other owner. Usual prices now pay more, whatever the other does. Both usual earns ₹5,000 each.

takeaway.line: The conflict is gone. Before “everyone should stop,” check what stopping alone changes—and what makes continuing attractive.
